Growth99 · Paid Media · Weight Management

Make the Support Visible

A Kenosha clinic wanted to reach patients who valued ongoing guidance. The medication was easy to describe. The harder job was to show what patients would get between appointments and why it mattered.

The Decision I Owned

I wrote the page around what patients could track and discuss at each check-in. Body composition gave readers a way to think about progress beyond weight alone. Food logs and nutrition feedback made the support concrete. Each detail gave readers a reason to consider the programme before they reached the booking form.

From the Brief to the Page

Strategy Brief · Summary

Attract patients who want medical guidance, feedback and accountability. Show what the programme includes beyond access to medication.

Landing Page · Original Section Headlines

“Medication Is One Part of the Plan”
“See What the Scale Cannot Show”
“For People Who Want Guidance, Not Just a Refill”

Client Approval, Launch and Revision

I handed off the copy on 28 October 2026. The team recorded client approval on 4 November and shared the updated live page on 5 November. After paid media flagged ad disapprovals, I added copy edits in Figma for review.

Brand Voice · Luxury

Fulton Brand and Homepage Copy

The Brief

Give alligator-leather high-tops and matching charms for people and their dogs a shared purpose on Fulton’s homepage.

The Approach

The founder’s story gave the copy its starting point. His German Shepherd, Rocco, chewed his sneakers. When a family allergy meant he had to give Rocco up, the two objects at the centre of the collection found their connection in that story.

The Brand Line

“Distance is not separation.”

Read the Fulton Copy Case Study

From About Copy to Brand Line

“Fulton believes that distance does not equate to separation.”

Early About Draft

The shorter line drops the brand name and gives the reader a direct statement to remember. The paired charms give it a physical expression. One stays with the person and the other with the dog.

How the Homepage Unfolds

The hero gives visitors a choice between Shop and Learn. The origin section introduces Rocco, then the high-top and craftsmanship sections bring the footwear into focus. The paired charms return the reader to the idea introduced in the brand line.

The Product Details

The footwear copy has specific details to work with, from round-scale alligator leather and hand stitching to the raised pattern on the rubber sole. Those details show what a reader can look for in the product.

At Growth99, I wrote towards a decision the reader could make that day. At Fulton, I wrote a line the brand could return to as the collection grew. Both briefs began with a feeling the reader could recognise.

How I Build Landing Pages

I start with the ad, the offer and the questions a reader brings to the page. I decide what the headline needs to say, what evidence backs up the offer and what the reader needs to know before they book. I built three tools to carry those decisions from the first brief to the final review.

SpaSage Prime V15

I start with inverse empathy mapping. If a patient hesitates because the consultation fee is unclear, I put the confirmed fee and what it covers beside the booking step. Marcus Sheridan’s question-first approach helps me give concerns about cost, suitability and recovery a place in the copy.

I use the Hero’s Journey to keep the reader at the centre and give the provider the role of guide. Classical rhetoric helps me decide where the page needs credibility, an emotional reason to care or evidence that supports the offer.

In Modify Mode, the 104-point editorial audit checks claim support, local SEO and the route from headline to CTA. The rationale log records what changed, which reader question the edit addresses and what evidence or approval the team still needs.

View SpaSage Prime V15 Showcase

SpaSage Master Codex

I wrote the SpaSage Master Codex as a system prompt that sets the rules for each task. It tells the model which inputs to use, what to return and which approved copy or claims to preserve during a revision.

I built Prompt Forge as the Codex’s rapid intake tool and use it within the Codex to turn an email or review notes into a task brief. The brief tells the model whether to draft a reply, write a new page or revise a live draft. For page optimisation, I specify which sections to change and ask for a log so I can review each edit.

SpaSage × Growth99 Four-Message Landing Page Guide

I designed this guide for LLMs with small context windows and tight token budgets. The writer enters the campaign facts once, then sends four messages in order in one drafting chat. Each drafting pass covers a defined set of page sections and has a word cap to help manage output length. A short handoff carries forward the heading, button and tag values, while fact IDs let the writer trace clinical claims back to the brief.

Fill the Campaign Brief

Record the legal business name, primary service, city and state for each location, phone number and provider credentials. Choose a service, membership or consultation page and state the offer in one sentence. Add four reader profiles with age and a decision driver, four sourced facts and the required disclaimer or compliance note. Use first names only for persona anchors.

Generate and Run the Four Messages

Give the completed brief to the configurator. Ask for exactly four labelled messages and no surrounding text. Each activation prompt should include the relevant slots, the approved fact ledger, the compliance note, house rules and a shared lexicon with eight phrases per persona. Use the same fact IDs and rules in both passes.

  1. Message 1 · Set up the first pass. Send the Single-Page Activation Prompt for S1 in a fresh drafting chat. Start with empty H2, BTN and TAG fields. Assign the SEO title, meta description, hero, two buttons and three value pillars to this pass.
  2. Message 2 · Draft the first pass. In the same chat, ask the model to fill the S1 slots within 450 words and return an @@ CAPSULE_OUT with its H2, BTN and TAG values. Keep the draft and its capsule.
  3. Message 3 · Pass the state forward. Paste the capsule values into the second activation prompt before sending it in the same chat. Assign services to S2. Assign candidacy, reasons to choose the provider, FAQs, closing copy and the footer blurb to S3.
  4. Message 4 · Draft the rest of the page. Ask the model to write S2 before S3 within 900 words and end with @@ CAPSULE_OUT. Combine these slots with S1. If either pass hits its limit, have the model finish the current slot, mark it with @@ STOPPED_AFTER [SLOT_ID] and return the capsule. Resume at the next slot.
Copy the Configurator Prompt and Brief 
Act as the SpaSage × Growth99 landing page configurator. Use the brief below to return exactly four messages, labelled MESSAGE 1 through MESSAGE 4, with no commentary or Markdown fences. Each activation prompt must define its output slots and their budgets. Ask for named slots only, with no template instructions in the copy itself.

MESSAGE 1: Build the S1 activation prompt. Start with empty H2, BTN and TAG state. Give each persona eight phrases and build a ledger with one stable ID per sourced fact. Include the compliance note and the editorial rules below. Define BTN_BOOK, BTN_EXPLORE, SEO_TITLE, META_DESC, H1, SUB, H2_PILLARS and PIL1–3_TITLE/TEXT.

MESSAGE 2: Execute Message 1. Fill the S1 slots. Cap the reply at 450 words and end with @@ CAPSULE_OUT followed by H2, BTN and TAG. If the cap prevents completion, end at a slot boundary and place @@ STOPPED_AFTER [SLOT_ID] before the capsule.

MESSAGE 3: Build the S2 and S3 activation prompt with a STATE FROM PREVIOUS OUTPUT placeholder for H2, BTN and TAG. Reuse the persona lexicon, rules and fact ledger from Message 1. For S2 define H2_SERVICES, SVC_INTRO and SVC1–3_TAG/DESC/CHK1/CHK2. For S3 define H2_CANDIDATES, CAND_INTRO, CAND1–3, H2_WHY, WHY1–3_TITLE/TEXT, H2_FAQ, FAQ1–4_Q/A, H2_CLOSE, CLOSE_TEXT and FOOT_BLURB. Expand numbered ranges into individual slot IDs.

MESSAGE 4: Execute Message 3. Write S2 before S3. Cap the reply at 900 words and use the same capsule and stop marker as Message 2.

EDITORIAL RULES: End each clinical sentence with {F:ID} from the fact ledger. Qualify outcomes where supported. Verify exact trademark and regulatory wording against the supplied sources. Use persona first names only and location terms only in permitted slots. Avoid em dashes and unapproved all-caps terms. Use at most one exclamation mark per 500 words. Apply the copy budgets and restricted terms supplied with this brief.

Carry the First Pass Into the Second

Copy the exact values from Message 2. Keep up to four headings and separate multiple entries with a vertical bar. The second pass can then refer to decisions already made about headings, buttons and recurring language.

STATE FROM PREVIOUS OUTPUT
H2: [heading 1 | heading 2]
BTN: [primary button | secondary button]
TAG: [approved tags from S1]

Set the Copy Budgets

Copy SlotBudgetWriting Rule
Buttons2–4 wordsStart with an action verb.
SEO Title and Meta DescriptionUp to 60 and 155 characters, respectivelyUse service and location in the title. Open the description with the benefit and invite a consultation.
Hero Headline and Subhead6–12 and 14–22 words, respectivelyLead with the benefit. Keep the location out of the H1 and add one concrete detail in the subhead.
H2s3–8 wordsUse title case.
Pillar and Benefit Blocks2–5 words per title, 15–25 per bodyLead the title with a noun and bold one phrase in the body.
Service Tags, Descriptions and Checks3–6, 35–55 and 12–20 words, respectivelyLead with the benefit. Use two sentences and one bold phrase in each description. Give each check a label and a sentence.
Candidacy Intro and Bullets10–25 words eachWrite a short intro and distinct bullets.
FAQ Questions and Answers5–12 and 40–60 words, respectivelyUse a patient’s question and one answer sentence that explains what varies.
Closing Copy and FooterUp to 70 words and 20–40 words, respectivelyUse three bold phrases in the close and two plain sentences in the footer.
Restricted Terms for This Workflow

Guaranteed, permanent, 100%, miracle, painless, pain-free, risk-free, safe, safest, evidence-based, proven, premier, leading, best, top-rated, instant, dramatic, anti-aging, FDA-approved, cure, eliminate, erase and fix.

Delve, explore, unpack, navigate, landscape, realm, tapestry, journey, robust, leverage, utilize, facilitate, seamless, cutting-edge and game-changer. Also flag “struggling with” and “embarrassed by” and keep “near me” out of body copy.

Run the Optional Slot Audit

Review the combined draft against the brief and its fact ledger. Check that each clinical sentence ends with its source tag ({F:ID}) and that each tag supports the sentence. Flag unsupported claims, guarantees, absolute outcomes and regulatory wording that lacks verification. Check trademark symbols against the approved names. Use qualified outcomes only where the evidence supports the wording.

Check house style, slot budgets and whether any labels meant for the template appear in the reader’s copy. Flag em dashes, unapproved all-caps terms, excess exclamation marks, banned words and locations outside their assigned slots. Ask for one PASS or FAIL per slot, a reason for each failure and a total. I verify any flagged claim against the source before the page goes to review.

The Approach

I start with the decision the audience faces. That gives the campaign a brief the team can write from, an idea it can build on and a clear reason for every section of the page.

  1. Frame the Decision

    I compare search intent and the ad’s promise with what the audience already knows. Then I work backwards from the action we want them to take. What would make them hesitate? What would they need to see before they felt ready? Those answers tell me which objection to address first and what proof belongs near the call to action.

  2. Find the Campaign Idea

    I look for a specific insight the brand can build a campaign around. For a laser hair removal page, that was the frustration of shaving or waxing only to start over. The idea gave the headline a recognisable moment and gave the rest of the page a job. It had to explain how the clinic plans treatment around the reader’s skin and hair.

  3. Test the Page in Order

    I read from ad to landing page to booking step. I check whether the first screen delivers on the ad, whether the proof arrives before the reader needs to act and whether the button makes the next step clear. I trace clinical claims to approved sources and flag any wording that needs a provider’s review.

  4. Give the Team a Usable Handoff

    I give design and marketing the copy hierarchy, the approved claim language and the reasoning behind the lead idea. If a section needs to shrink for mobile or the campaign needs a new ad, the team can see which parts carry the promise and where they have room to adapt.
